gao-gaoreports-gao-05-1008t:
Patent office strain is the topic of GAO-05-1008T, a statement given on September 8, 2005. The U.S. Patent and Trademark Office grants the patents that guard new ideas. Yet yearly filings rose from about 185,000 to over 350,000 in ten years. A backlog of about 750,000 filings built up. Filings were set to top 450,000 by 2009.

The statement sums up two June 2005 GAO reports. One weighs the office's push to handle filings by computer. The other weighs its hard task of hiring and keeping skilled patent staff. Both tracks shape how fast and how well patents get checked.
gao-gaoreports-gao-05-1048t:
Human Capital, GAO-05-1048T of September 27, 2005, draws on a March 2005 forum on how to pay federal staff by market rates and job results. The federal pay system still sorts, pays, and spurs staff much as it did decades ago. Reform talk centers on tying pay more to skill demand and to work well done.

GAO and top personnel chiefs ran the forum. Public, private, and charity groups shared what worked and what failed. The statement lists the paths those groups chose to design new pay plans. It also shows how they put the plans in place and kept staff trust while pay rules changed.
gao-gaoreports-gao-05-258t:
Digital Broadcast Television Transition, GAO-05-258T of February 17, 2005, prices a grant that could speed the shift to digital TV. When the shift ends, old air waves free up for new wireless use and for safety crews. A set-top box can turn digital waves into a form old sets can show. Some urge a public grant for such boxes.

GAO sorts homes by how they watch TV now. It notes how those groups split by age, cash, and race. It lists the gear each home would need. It then prices a box grant in a range of ways, with set rules on who would count.
gao-gaoreports-gao-05-358t:
Mass Transit, GAO-05-358T of February 18, 2005, gives early facts on the federal stake in the capital's rail and bus arm. The Washington Metropolitan Area Transit Authority runs Metrorail for the city and its ring. Use stands at an all-time high. Cash strain, and fears on safety and sound runs, press the arm at the same time. The tale here rests on work still in train.

GAO tells how far federal cash built the subway, and why the state paid. It tells how far such cash has backed fresh build work of late. It lays out the cash tests the arm now faces, and the paths pitched to meet them.
gao-gaoreports-gao-05-428t:
The Army's Future Combat Systems program is examined in testimony GAO-05-428T, presented on March 16, 2005. FCS was a planned $108 billion set of 18 manned and unmanned vehicles, aircraft, sensors, and munitions tied together by one network. Development began in May 2003, and the program was reshaped in July 2004. GAO was asked to weigh the technical and management challenges, the odds of delivery on cost and schedule, and options for moving ahead.

GAO said the program's scale created hard problems in requirements, development, finance, and management. Vehicles had to be lighter than current ones yet just as lethal and survivable. Nearly two years after launch, with $4.6 billion spent, requirements were still not firm. Only 1 of more than 50 technologies was mature. GAO judged the program at high risk of missing its cost and capability goals. The testimony lays out those risks for Congress.
gao-gaoreports-gao-05-448t:
Seaport security more than three years after the September 11 attacks is surveyed in testimony GAO-05-448T, presented on May 17, 2005. Ports are large, open by land and water, and close to cities. They also form a key link in the world supply chain. GAO summed up past work on steps taken to guard ports, the main problems found, and tools that could help plan the next steps.

Federal agencies had stepped up ship tracking, cargo checks, and patrols. Port owners and local police had assessed weak points and put security plans in place. But the rush to act left gaps. Plans often lacked clear goals and measures of progress. Coordinating many agencies and private owners proved hard. Keeping funds in place over time was also a concern. The testimony helps readers judge whether port security gains could last.
gao-gaoreports-gao-05-648t:
Open government requests are tracked in GAO testimony GAO-05-648T, dated May 11, 2005. The Freedom of Information Act lets anyone ask agencies for records. Most take requests in writing, though some accept them by phone or online. Demand climbed fast: requests rose 71 percent from 2002 to 2004. Agencies processed 68 percent more requests in the same span. In 2004 they handed over full records in 92 percent of finished cases.

The queue still grows. Pending requests carried into the next year rose 14 percent since 2002. The testimony walks through each step of handling a request, from intake to release, and compares how the 25 largest agencies report their numbers.
gao-gaoreports-gao-05-688t:
GAO-05-688T of May 10, 2005 restates, as testimony, the embassy soft-target findings of the report issued a day earlier. Since 1968, 32 U.S. officials have been attacked outside embassies, 23 fatally. The State Department guards homes and schools and briefs staff, yet has no full strategy for life beyond the compound walls. A draft effort had just begun, with legal and money questions open.

Three attack inquiries demanded hands-on counterterror training and firm compliance checks. The course remains optional and the checks weak, GAO testifies. A school safety program holds $29.8 million from fiscal 2003 and 2004, with its scope still unset.
gao-gaoreports-gao-05-698t:
Amtrak's troubled Acela trains frame GAO testimony GAO-05-698T, dated May 11, 2005. The high-speed sets, ordered in 1996, hit design faults and delays from the start. In April 2005 brake cracks pulled every set from service, cutting Amtrak's richest revenue line. Amtrak and its builders sued each other for $200 million apiece before settling in March 2004. The deal's warranties shield Amtrak, but lost ticket money is not recoverable.

Amtrak is set to take over upkeep in October 2006. GAO warns it lacks proven skill and funds for the job, and draws lessons for big projects.
gao-gaoreports-gao-05-718t:
Keeping shuttle skills alive until the fleet retires is the subject of GAO testimony GAO-05-718T (May 18, 2005). The shuttle must finish building the space station before it stands down. The March 2005 GAO report behind this testimony found NASA short on a long-term workforce plan. The program had gathered lessons from other fleets' retirements, and its main contractor had begun preparing. But the press of returning the shuttle to flight crowded out planning.

Staff may drift away without a clear path past retirement, and bonus money is unsure. Delays now, GAO warns, risk blown schedules later.
gao-gaoreports-gao-05-778t:
Federal paperwork burden is the theme of testimony GAO-05-778T, delivered June 14, 2005. Americans spend billions of hours each year on federal forms and surveys. The Paperwork Reduction Act aims to cut that load while keeping the data useful. The budget office must clear each collection and report yearly on burden. Agency tech chiefs must also certify each form.

GAO said total burden fell slightly in fiscal year 2004. The estimate was 7.971 billion hours, down 1.6 percent. But the figures rest on shaky estimates, so small shifts mean little. In case studies, tech chiefs certified forms even when support for the claim was thin or missing. GAO argued that cutting burden may take a new approach.
gao-gaoreports-gao-05-788t:
U.S. work to guard ideas abroad is described in testimony GAO-05-788T from June 14, 2005. Piracy and fakes hit U.S. goods in many lands. Several agencies work to lift protection overseas. GAO drew on a past report and fresh work. It laid out what agencies do and how they coordinate. It also weighed the impact so far and the blocks that remain.

GAO found that U.S. efforts have helped strengthen laws abroad. Tools include a yearly review naming the worst problem countries, training for foreign officials, and seizures of fake goods. A council set up in 1999 to align the work has had little impact. Its leader post sat empty. A 2004 anti-piracy strategy added some new steps. Enforcement, GAO said, remains the hard part.
gao-gaoreports-gao-05-838t:
Courthouse building costs are summed up in testimony GAO-05-838T, delivered June 21, 2005. A federal buildings fund pays for courthouses. The judiciary pays rent into that fund. Rent now eats a growing share of the judiciary's budget. In December 2004, judges asked for a $483 million yearly rent exemption. GAO reviewed 20 years of its courthouse work for this testimony.

GAO recalled that loose choices in the 1990s led to costly features in some courthouses. Long-range space forecasts proved unreliable back then. Courtroom use was not tracked well enough to judge sharing. The buildings fund has never raised enough for repairs. Its backlog hit $5.7 billion by 2002. The testimony also frames GAO's live review of the rent request.
gao-gaoreports-gao-05-848t:
Federal real property reform is urged in testimony GAO-05-848T, given June 22, 2005. GAO placed this area on its high-risk list in January 2003. The flaws are old: spare and worn buildings, shaky data, and costly leased space. Terror risk adds a new strain. The testimony lays out the problems and what must be done.

Over 30 agencies hold hundreds of thousands of assets worth hundreds of billions of dollars. Many no longer fit their agencies' missions. Repair needs run to tens of billions of dollars. Costly leasing fills gaps that ownership could serve. In February 2004, the President ordered agencies to name senior property officers and set priorities. A new council at the budget office is building shared principles and a joint inventory. GAO said further actions are still needed.
gao-gaoreports-gao-05-928t:
Restricted airspace breaches are reviewed in testimony GAO-05-928T, delivered July 21, 2005. Guarding U.S. airspace is a shared mission across agencies. GAO was asked for the threat picture, breach counts since 2001, and agency steps and procedures. A classified report was due later in the year. To stay unclassified, the testimony skips the threat assessment.

The aviation agency counted about 3,400 breaches from September 12, 2001, to December 31, 2004. Most were by general aviation pilots. Causes include weather detours and new restrictions set with little warning. Some pilots simply fail to check notices. Terrorists could also probe the response, GAO noted. Agencies have raised screening and patrols, and run a joint capital center. But GAO found gaps in the fast, multi-agency response when a breach occurs. Management fixes are needed, it said.
gao-gaoreports-gao-05-998t:
The Defense Travel System gets early audit views in testimony GAO-05-998T, presented September 29, 2005. The department has spent 10 years building a single end-to-end travel system. Congress has pressed on travel practice throughout. GAO's audit runs under the Comptroller General's own authority. The testimony gives early results on three questions, plus the department's rights in the system.

GAO found testing of key functions was weak. Flaws surfaced only after deployment, and the schedule slipped badly. Testing gave no sound assurance that flight and fare data display correctly. Bad interface tests let the fault through. Travelers may have paid more as a result. The system fixed a duplicate payment flaw, GAO found. But premium class misuse, unused tickets not refunded, and claim errors remain. Two hurdles stand out: building needed interfaces, and low use at sites that have the system.
gao-gaoreports-gao-06-1008t:
Medicare doctor pay and its fee formula are discussed in testimony GAO-06-1008T, given July 25, 2006. A growth-rate system sets yearly fee changes. In 2002, it cut fees by almost 5 percent. Later actions blocked cuts from 2003 through 2006. Without new action, cuts are projected from 2007 through 2015. The formula's fitness is now in doubt.

The statement explains how the system tries to hold down spending growth. It explains why fees are set to fall under it. It tracks use of doctor services and spending from 2000 through 2005. It closes with options to revise or replace the system. The work rests on two GAO reports, one issued July 21, 2006. Rising service use sits at the heart of the debate the testimony frames.
gao-gaoreports-gao-06-1028t:
The individual income tax is weighed for reform in testimony GAO-06-1028T, given August 3, 2006. Income and payroll taxes supply about 80 percent of federal revenue. Long-range forecasts show revenues and spending drifting apart without policy change. Debate turns on two paths: fix the income tax with a broader base and flatter rates, or move to a consumption tax. The testimony rests on past GAO work and literature.

GAO reviews what the income tax brings in. It then weighs its complexity, its drag on the economy, its fairness, and compliance issues. It sets out common yardsticks for comparing reform plans. It draws conclusions for the reform debate from that record. Streamlining, simplification, and further reforms are all desirable, the title holds. The testimony gives lawmakers the tests to apply to any plan.
gao-gaoreports-gao-06-1058t:
A fresh Capitol Visitor Center update is testimony GAO-06-1058T, delivered September 21, 2006. A Senate appropriations panel last heard on the project on August 2, 2006. The Architect of the Capitol runs the build with a construction manager. GAO reviewed schedules and money reports, watched the site, and spoke with the project team, fire officials, and Capitol Police.

The testimony reports progress on set milestones since the August hearing. It gives GAO's assessment of the currently scheduled completion date. It updates the expected cost at completion and the funding picture. Key challenges and risks that still face the project are named. So are the actions GAO believes the Architect must take to hold the current date. The update aids the panel's close monitoring of the build.
gao-gaoreports-gao-06-208t:
The tax gap and how to shrink it are argued in GAO-06-208T, testimony presented on October 26, 2005. The gap is the split between taxes owed under law and taxes paid on time and in full. It grows through underreported income, unpaid bills, and unfiled returns. The Internal Revenue Service put the 2001 gap at $312 billion to $353 billion. After later collections, the net gap stood at $257 billion to $298 billion. Even a 1 percent cut would yield over $2.5 billion a year.

GAO urged attack on many fronts at once: a simpler code, good taxpayer service, and firm enforcement. Withholding and information reporting do much of the work. The agency's data on parts of the gap rest on old studies, though. It lacks fresh compliance data for several parts. It also lacks clear long-term goals for closing the gap. GAO said steady measurement and set targets must anchor the fight.
gao-gaoreports-gao-06-228t:
A decade of GAO work on federal rulemaking is summed up in GAO-06-228T, testimony dated November 1, 2005. Agencies issue thousands of rules each year on safety, pollution, taxes, and more. Over ten years GAO wrote more than 60 reports and statements on how those rules get made. This statement draws out the shared themes. It flags where Congress may want to act or study further.

Review rules bring real gains, GAO found: more public voice, clearer process, and stronger analysis behind rules. Four flaws blunt them: vague terms, patchy coverage, uneven agency practice, and a focus on one stage only. Presidential review of rules has grown stronger over time. Congress's own tool, a disapproval process, has had less effect. Agencies also skip public notice more often, sometimes with thin reasons. GAO named four areas that merit fresh attention from lawmakers.
gao-gaoreports-gao-06-248t:
Surplus federal buildings and land are the focus of GAO-06-248T, testimony presented on February 6, 2006. GAO named federal real property a high-risk area in January 2003 and updated that call in January 2005. Idle and half-used property is a chief reason for the label. The government holds a vast stock of sites it no longer needs. Keeping them drains funds that real missions could use. This statement reviews why the surplus pile persists.

Agencies cling to space for many reasons. Disposal rules are slow, and sites can carry cleanup costs or local pushback. Data on what the government owns stay shaky, so leaders cannot see the full pile. GAO surveys the steps taken so far to shed surplus sites. It then sets out what more must happen. The testimony keeps a slow problem in view: a government that cannot quit unneeded property pays for it every year.
gao-gaoreports-gao-06-318t:
The visitor tracking program US-VISIT, up and running yet still rough, anchors GAO-06-318T, testimony given January 25, 2006. The system gathers facts and biometric markers on some foreign visitors. Finger scans and photos screen travelers against watch lists. They confirm a visitor matches the visa presented. Exit checks at set ports aim to log departures the same way. GAO testified on the program's current state. It also graded the department's progress on advice from past reviews of yearly spending plans.

Management improvements are still needed, GAO said. Its advice targets the department's ability to deliver the system on time and within budget. The department has said the advice made the program stronger. This statement draws on earlier reports and on fresh work for the House homeland security panel. Each hearing marks which promises have been kept and which remain open.
gao-gaoreports-gao-06-398t:
Small towns can lose air service as airlines chase stronger markets. Testimony GAO-06-398T, given September 14, 2006, reviews federal aid for small community air service. Network carriers faced hard finances over the prior decade. Low-cost carriers drew passengers from some small airports. Congress set up two funding programs in response. They are Essential Air Service and the Small Community Air Service Development Program.

GAO traced the growth and effect of the first program. It gave the status of the second. It also set out options to reform one and judge the other. The testimony rests on past GAO research and program updates. Readers get costs, results, and choices.
gao-gaoreports-gao-06-418t:
Before a Senate panel, GAO made the same case for its yearly funds. In testimony GAO-06-418T (April 26, 2006), Comptroller General David M Walker supports GAO's fiscal year 2007 request. The request seeks $509.4 million in budget authority. That is a 5 percent rise over the revised fiscal year 2006 level. It supports 3,267 full-time equivalent staff, 50 more than planned.

A table of performance measures opens the statement. It tracks financial benefits, timeliness, and past recommendations put in place. Walker cites peer reviews and gains in audit work at home and abroad. Readers see both the money asked and the results claimed. The panel was the Senate appropriations group for the legislative branch.
gao-gaoreports-gao-06-428t:
Rebuilding a war-torn country while a new government forms is the backdrop here. Testimony GAO-06-428T, given February 8, 2006, covers U.S. work to stabilize and rebuild Iraq. The effort ran in an unstable security setting. Iraq was moving toward its first permanent government. The U.S. goal was a democratic, stable, and prosperous Iraq at peace with its neighbors.

GAO discusses challenges the United States faces in rebuilding work. It also covers challenges the Iraqi government faces in paying for future needs. The statement rests on four GAO reports since July 2005 and recent trips. Topics include water and sanitation, elections aid, and security. Readers get a broad status check.
gao-gaoreports-gao-06-448t:
A service with rescue, security, and sea duties faced a tight budget year. Testimony GAO-06-448T, given June 15, 2006, gives GAO views on the Coast Guard. The service asked for $8.4 billion for fiscal year 2007. That is a rise of 4 percent, or $328 million, over the approved fiscal year 2006 budget. Growth was slowing after two years of larger rises.

GAO sums up current and past reviews. It covers performance goals and added duties. It gives special note to Deepwater, which replaces cutters and aircraft. It also covers Rescue 21, a rescue communications upgrade. Readers see operations and future challenges in one statement.
gao-gaoreports-gao-06-458t:
Fake numbers can let people work without legal permission. GAO's GAO-06-458T testimony, delivered February 16, 2006, covers Social Security numbers and unauthorized work. A valid number is required to work lawfully. Noncitizens also need work approval from the Department of Homeland Security. Some workers have gained jobs with false information. Congress asked GAO how agencies can share earnings data better.

GAO names Social Security data that could help spot unauthorized work. It also studies coordination among federal agencies. Better sharing could make the data more accurate and useful. A coordinated approach could help cut unauthorized work, GAO said. Readers see a data problem with direct job effects.
gao-gaoreports-gao-06-478t:
The Army's future combat network would cost on the order of $200 billion with related programs. Testimony GAO-06-478T, dated March 1, 2006, returns to the Future Combat System. The system is a networked family of weapons and other gear. It sits at the front of the Army's push to become lighter and faster. Defense planned investment in new systems had doubled in five years. Research costs on new weapons kept growing by 30 to 40 percent.

GAO discusses the business case the program needs to succeed. It also covers the business arrangements that support that case. Money pressure is a core theme. Readers get the fiscal frame for a huge program.
gao-gaoreports-gao-06-528t:
One month after a hearing, GAO updated Congress on a visitor center's cost and schedule. Delivered March 15, 2006, testimony GAO-06-528T reports the Capitol Visitor Center's status as of that day. It follows a February 15, 2006 hearing on the project. The Architect of the Capitol runs the project. GAO discusses progress toward selected milestones since the hearing. It also covers how the schedule has been managed in that span.

Key challenges and risks still face the project, GAO notes. It lists actions the architect has taken or plans to meet them. It also gives the status of project costs and funding. Readers get a dated snapshot, useful beside the February analysis.
gao-gaoreports-gao-06-548t:
The Army was rebuilding itself into smaller, self-contained brigades. The testimony numbered GAO-06-548T, delivered April 4, 2006, assesses the Army modular force. The shift from divisions to modular brigades is the largest restructuring since World War II. Modular brigades are meant to deploy faster and work better in joint operations. The change needs extensive equipment spending and retraining. GAO based the statement on past and current work, focused on active forces.

GAO addresses the Army's cost estimate for the change. It reports progress and plans for equipping brigade teams. It covers personnel needs and how results will be judged. Capabilities and cost remain uncertain, GAO said.
gao-gaoreports-gao-06-558t:
Detectors must be placed abroad and at home to stop nuclear smuggling. The testimony numbered GAO-06-558T, delivered March 28, 2006, sums up two GAO reports released that day. Together with a March 2005 report, they cover the worldwide deployment effort. The Energy, Defense, and State departments provide detection gear to foreign countries. The Homeland Security Department installs gear at U.S. ports of entry. Each side faces its own challenges.

GAO discusses progress and problems in the foreign programs. It then turns to the domestic installation effort. Readers get the full deployment picture in one statement. The testimony links overseas and border work as parts of one shield.
gao-gaoreports-gao-06-578t:
Fraud control in Medicaid gets a new federal program, and this statement sizes it up. On March 28, 2006, testimony GAO-06-578T covered the Medicaid Integrity Program. Medicaid covers over 56 million low-income people. In fiscal year 2004 it paid $287 billion in benefits. The federal share was about $168 billion. States hold the main duty for stopping bad payments. The federal Medicare and Medicaid agency supports and oversees state work.

GAO focuses on concerns about federal help to states. It explains how the new program expands that help. It names challenges the agency must address as it starts the program. New federal leadership chances are the theme.
gao-gaoreports-gao-06-588t:
A second April statement updates early results on gas pipeline checks. Testimony GAO-06-588T, dated April 27, 2006, gives preliminary observations on the gas integrity management program. About a dozen people are killed or injured in gas transmission pipeline incidents each year. A 2002 law requires checks on segments in about 20,000 miles of busy areas. Half of the first checks are due by December 2007. The rest are due by December 2012. Operators must repair flawed pipe and recheck at least every seven years.

GAO reports early results on the program's safety effects. It covers the seven-year recheck rule as well. It also discusses stronger enforcement after GAO's 2004 advice. Two fuller reports were expected that fall.
gao-gaoreports-gao-06-598t:
Technology is central to a new department's mission and to its makeover. Testimony GAO-06-598T, dated March 29, 2006, reviews information technology management at the Department of Homeland Security. GAO has named the department's setup and transformation as high risk. To use technology well, the department needs strong controls. Those include an enterprise architecture and portfolio-based choices among rival projects. GAO has made many recommendations on both levels. This testimony rests on that body of work.

GAO covers the state of technology management across the department. It also covers single investment projects. Progress continues, GAO said, but challenges remain. Readers see why controls must come before systems.
gao-gaoreports-gao-06-608t:
Trade with China is the focus of GAO testimony GAO-06-608T, given on April 4, 2006. Some United States firms claimed that unfair subsidies helped China sell goods in United States markets. Firms hurt by subsidized imports can often seek countervailing duties, which are extra charges on those imports. The United States did not apply such duties to China, which it classed as a non-market economy.

The testimony, based on a June 2005 GAO report, lays out the options for applying these duties to China. It also sets out the hard choices and legal hurdles that would arise. GAO then weighs what the likely results would be for United States firms and buyers. Readers get a plain map of a tough trade policy choice.
gao-gaoreports-gao-06-628t:
Low national saving and its long-term risks are the theme of GAO-06-628T, testimony GAO gave on April 6, 2006. National saving is the share of national income that is not consumed. It comes from households, businesses, and all levels of government. Saving funds the investment that replaces old plants and buys better equipment. Higher saving and investment lift productivity and growth over time.

GAO warned that current saving choices carry deep effects for the nation's future well-being. Low saving leaves less capital for growth and more reliance on foreign funds. GAO linked saving to the federal budget deficit and to household choices. The testimony frames saving as a choice that shapes living standards for decades.
gao-gaoreports-gao-06-698t:
The FBI's Trilogy computer upgrade is examined in GAO-06-698T, testimony GAO presented on May 2, 2006. Begun in 2001, Trilogy was the bureau's largest technology upgrade to date. It did deliver updated networks and desktop systems across the bureau. But it failed to upgrade the investigative applications agents use to manage cases. Missed milestones and cost growth plagued the project for years.

GAO told the Senate panel that weak controls led to payment of questionable contractor costs. Assets bought under the project also went missing. The bureau lacked firm checks on contractor bills and property records. GAO's account shows how poor project control can waste funds even when parts of a system reach users. The testimony fed wider concern over federal technology management.
gao-gaoreports-gao-06-738t:
Air traffic modernization gets an earlier status check in GAO-06-738T, testimony presented on May 4, 2006. The Federal Aviation Administration's upgrade program had been on GAO's high-risk list for over a decade. Two newer offices now lead the work. The Air Traffic Organization runs today's system, and a joint planning office designs the next generation system. GAO updated Congress on both fronts.

GAO said the Air Traffic Organization had made promising moves toward a results focus. Its culture, management, and buying processes were improving. But the office was only slightly more than two years old. GAO warned that the new processes were not yet firmly rooted. It was also too early to judge the planning for the next generation system. Steady follow-through, GAO said, would decide the outcome.
gao-gaoreports-gao-06-748t:
Companion concerns on contractor clearances appear in GAO-06-748T, testimony GAO delivered on May 17, 2006. Like its pair, the statement covers the Defense Department's roughly 2 million active clearances. About one-third of them serve industry personnel who work under federal contracts. GAO shared preliminary observations from its ongoing audit of the clearance system. The focus here falls on fresh problems that had lately emerged.

GAO said new concerns were slowing the processing of industry clearances. One threat was the possible expiration of the executive order that underpins the system. That lapse could slow recent improvements in clearance work. The statement also repeats the strain from high request volume and tight funding. Together, the two statements map a clearance system under pressure from several directions at once.
gao-gaoreports-gao-06-808t:
The military's Katrina response is summed up in GAO-06-808T, testimony GAO presented on May 25, 2006. Katrina was one of the largest natural disasters in United States history. Despite a huge deployment at every level, many judged the federal response to be inadequate. This statement distills GAO's report on the military side of that response. It covers planning, exercises, and the actions taken once the storm hit.

GAO said pre-storm preparations had not fully addressed the capabilities a catastrophic disaster demands. The military response was massive, yet it faced several serious challenges. Ad hoc tasking and unclear roles slowed parts of the effort. The Defense Department had begun corrective steps, some of them complex and long-standing. GAO's core call was for better plans and exercises to guide the next response.
gao-gaoreports-gao-06-828t:
The Capitol Visitor Center saga continues in GAO-06-828T, testimony presented on August 2, 2006. GAO again reviewed milestones and schedule management, this time since the June 28, 2006 hearing. It also tracked the actions the Architect of the Capitol took on known risks. At the June hearing, the project had just pushed back its completion dates. Lawmakers wanted to know whether the new dates would hold.

GAO said construction kept moving forward over the summer. The overall target dates stayed about the same as reported in June. But risks had materialized, above all in the fire protection system. A number of important activities had slipped. Those delays lessened GAO's confidence in the likelihood of meeting the targets. The testimony keeps the pressure on a troubled project.
gao-gaoreports-gao-06-868t:
Mortgage insurance reform is weighed in GAO-06-868T, testimony presented on June 20, 2006. The Federal Housing Administration insures home loans for buyers who cannot get plain market credit. It had faced rising default rates and higher than expected program costs. Participation in its programs had also fallen sharply. The housing department proposed reforms to the National Housing Act to help the agency adapt. GAO shared its past findings on the risks those changes would raise.

GAO said past work found weaknesses in how the agency manages risk and estimates costs. Its mortgage scorecard, a tool that grades borrower default risk, was generally reasonable. Yet the way the scorecard was built and used limited its value. GAO warned that the proposed reforms will heighten the need for better risk work. Bigger lending powers demand sharper cost estimates.
gao-gaoreports-gao-06-878t:
Crop insurance fraud, waste, and abuse are the subject of GAO testimony GAO-06-878T, dated June 15, 2006. The federal crop program is run by the Risk Management Agency with private insurers. In 2005 it cost $2.7 billion. About $117 million of that was lost to fraud, waste, and abuse.

The testimony rests on GAO's September 30, 2005 report on the same program. GAO weighed new tools from the Agricultural Risk Protection Act of 2000, such as sanction power and field checks. It urged better field checks, recovery of bad payments, tighter watch on insurers, and rules for wider sanction use.
gao-gaoreports-gao-06-888t:
Nuclear plant safety oversight gets a second GAO look in testimony GAO-06-888T, dated June 19, 2006. The Nuclear Regulatory Commission must ensure the nation's 103 commercial plants run safely. Since 2000 it has used a Reactor Oversight Process built to focus on the gravest risks.

Like its companion statement days before, the testimony is early work, with a full report to come later. GAO drew on five years of process results and close study of 11 plants. It set out how oversight works, what the results show, and which parts need to improve. It also notes the steps NRC had taken so far.
gao-gaoreports-gao-06-948t:
New ways to gauge student growth under the No Child Left Behind Act are the topic of GAO testimony GAO-06-948T, dated July 27, 2006. The law asks all students to reach skill in reading and math by 2014, with gaps between groups closed. States had set yearly targets from one year's scores.

Some states wanted growth models, which track score change over time. GAO told how many states used them, and for what ends. It showed how growth models can track progress toward the law's aims. It also set out the strain states face in using them well. The testimony rests on a recent GAO report.
gao-gaoreports-gao-06-998t:
Small firms and the weight of federal rules are the theme of GAO testimony GAO-06-998T, dated July 20, 2006. The Regulatory Flexibility Act of 1980 tells agencies to weigh how rules hit small firms, small towns, and small charities. A 1996 update and a 2002 order sought to firm up that duty.

Doubts on rule burden persist, and bills to amend the act were in play. GAO summed up the act's aim and terms. It drew out the chief blocks its past work found in the act's use. It named parts Congress might revisit and clear up, to make the act work better.
gao-gaoreports-gao-07-1038t:
Licenses for radioactive sources can still be gamed, GAO states in testimony GAO-07-1038T, dated July 12, 2007. Sealed sources serve in medicine, industry, and research. Buyers need a license from the Nuclear Regulatory Commission or from a state with a like program.

In 2003 GAO warned that weak licensing could let terrorists get such stock. The regulator issued new guidance to license reviewers in reply. A Senate panel then asked GAO to test the system in secret. The steps taken since 2003, GAO found, are not effective. The testimony is a rare public record of an undercover audit of a safety gate.
gao-gaoreports-gao-07-1098t:
Deep flaws in federal buying need care, GAO states in testimony GAO-07-1098T, dated July 17, 2007. In fiscal year 2006 the government spent over $400 billion on goods and services. The Defense Department is the largest buyer. With a large budget gap, each buy must earn its keep.

GAO has named four contract fields as high risk across the government. The testimony draws out four core hurdles. Buyers must split wants from needs. They must set and back sound program terms. They must use contractors aptly, as a tool. They must build a skilled workforce and hold it to account. The record spans decades of GAO findings.
gao-gaoreports-gao-07-1108t:
Shared medical data between two big departments is updated in GAO testimony GAO-07-1108T, dated July 18, 2007. The Veterans Affairs and Defense departments work to swap health facts. Good swaps aid care for active troops and veterans alike. Both build new systems that hold data in forms computers can act on, such as drug allergy alerts.

GAO summed up the past and current state of that work. It covered long-term system builds. It covered short-term steps with systems now in use. The base is prior GAO work, plus papers and talks with both departments. Headway is real, GAO said, but full electronic records stay far off.
gao-gaoreports-gao-07-1228t:
Six years after the World Trade Center attack, many responders still faced health problems from the site. This testimony is GAO-07-1228T, dated September 18, 2007. It updates GAO's July 2007 report on health services for those responders. It covers federal screening for responders who were federal workers. It also covers services for nonfederal responders living outside the New York City area.

GAO reported that the federal screening program had a troubled history. Health officials set it up in June 2003, suspended it in March 2004, then resumed it in December 2005. By September 2006, it had screened 907 federal workers. GAO said the health department had not yet answered its call to ensure services for all responders. It also noted $51 million in treatment funds awarded or set aside from a $75 million appropriation.
gao-gaoreports-gao-07-1248t:
Every full-power television station must switch to digital-only broadcasts on February 17, 2009. GAO gave early findings on viewer education for that switch in GAO-07-1248T on September 19, 2007. Households using antennas on analog sets must act or lose service. A federal program offers coupons toward converter boxes that keep old sets working. GAO spoke with broadcast regulators, the coupon program agency, and industry groups.

GAO described education efforts already under way and others being planned. The coupon program holds $1.5 billion in federal funds. From January 1, 2008, households may request up to two $40 coupons. The testimony flags problems that could hamper outreach efforts. It also previews GAO's ongoing work on public awareness of the change. GAO stressed that its findings at this stage are preliminary.
gao-gaoreports-gao-07-1258t:
The Marshall Islands depend on U.S. aid that is set to shrink year by year. In GAO-07-1258T, dated September 25, 2007, GAO weighed the islands' path to self-reliance. An amended compact gives the country about $1.5 billion from 2004 to 2023. Grants fall over time while payments build a trust fund. That fund must support the budget after grants end in 2023. The Interior Department oversees the aid.

GAO said both governments had set up the new compact rules and reporting. But the islands had made little progress on reforms to grow private business and tax income. The economy still rests heavily on government spending of foreign aid. GAO's modeling showed the trust fund could fall short in some later years. Under a moderate investment path, shortfall odds rose from about 10 percent by 2031 to almost 40 percent by 2050.
gao-gaoreports-gao-07-208t:
The Pentagon built one travel system to handle trips and vouchers for the whole department. GAO questioned its promised savings in testimony GAO-07-208T on November 16, 2006. The Defense Travel System began in 1995. The testimony rests on GAO's September 2006 report. GAO tested the math in a 2003 economic study of the system. It also checked use rates and known faults in how the system works.

The study claimed $54.1 million a year in staff savings for fiscal years 2009 through 2016. GAO found the key assumptions behind that figure invalid. Staff shifted to other work do not save the department money. A core measure of hands-off processing also fell short. The hoped-for rate was 70 percent; actual results were at best 47 percent. GAO said the department lacked sound metrics for system use. It urged fixes to function and tracking alike.
gao-gaoreports-gao-07-358t:
Other governments bargain hard on drug prices, and this testimony catalogs their tools. GAO delivered the survey in testimony GAO-07-358T on January 11, 2007. The statement grows out of GAO reports from 2002 through 2006. It covers foreign government methods first. It then covers U.S. private payers. It ends with federal programs besides Medicare Part D. The backdrop is debate over letting Medicare negotiate prices.

Foreign tools include outright price ceilings, GAO reports. Some states set one price for groups of similar drugs. Others cap drug makers' profits and claw back excess. U.S. health plans hire benefit managers to bargain. Those managers pass back rebates and win pharmacy discounts. Mail-order dispensing cuts costs further. Plans also steer patients toward cheaper drugs. Federal health plans use the same levers. The testimony draws no single model for Part D.
gao-gaoreports-gao-07-378t:
The border fingerprint program's land-crossing rollout drew a second airing before Congress. GAO-07-378T, testimony dated January 31, 2007, restates GAO's December 2006 report. GAO staff visited 21 land crossings on both borders. The testimony covers entry screening, exit tracking, and program fit. Entry checks were live at most crossings by then.

The testimony stresses the exit problem. Radio-tag trials failed to detect most travelers' tags, GAO said. Tags cannot prove the holder is the person who entered. That fails the law's biometric exit demand. Computer faults hit 12 of the visited crossings. At 9 of them, staff did not always report the faults. A planned passport card would use the same radio technology. Key choices about travel documents were still open. GAO urged stronger controls and land-specific measures.
gao-gaoreports-gao-07-398t: The homeland department's growing pains persisted in 2007, and GAO's briefing again lists the management and program challenges. The testimony repeats the inventory. The findings warn that the young giant was still finding its footing. The growing had to become governing.
gao-gaoreports-gao-07-418t: Stopping disaster-aid fraud before it started was the 2007 lesson, and GAO's briefing says prevention was the key to minimizing waste in the recovery. The testimony makes the case. The findings warn that the storm money needed locks, not just audits. The fraud had to be stopped at the door.
gao-gaoreports-gao-07-428t: The nuclear weapons agency needed better security habits in 2007, and GAO's briefing says improvements could sharpen a key implementation. The testimony presses the point. The findings warn that the bomb-makers' house needed stronger locks. The arsenal deserved airtight management.
gao-gaoreports-gao-07-448t: Screening flyers was getting more planned in 2007, and GAO's briefing says the planning was guiding the big money choices, with more work left. The briefing mixes credit and caution. The findings warn that the sky's shield needed more work. The plans had to turn into real shields.
gao-gaoreports-gao-07-488t: Closing the tax gap needed many tools in 2007, and GAO's briefing says multiple approaches were required to shrink the shortfall. The testimony lays out the arsenal. The findings warn that the hundreds of billions owed would not collect themselves. The gap was measured in hundreds of billions.
gao-gaoreports-gao-07-558t: Kids' health insurance was up for renewal in 2007, and GAO's briefing reviews the states' enrollment and spending experience. The testimony previews the reauthorization fight. The findings ask whether the program covering millions of children would survive. The children's coverage hung in the balance.
gao-gaoreports-gao-07-638t: Yellowstone's bison plan got an early grade in 2007, and GAO's briefing previews how the interagency herd management was going. The testimony watches the wildlife politics closely. The findings ask whether the buffalo and the ranchers could ever truly share the range.
gao-gaoreports-gao-07-698t: Katrina contracting data was full of holes in 2007 — GAO's briefing says the records on subcontracting chances for small firms needed completing. The testimony demands the full picture. The findings ask whether the storm's rebuilding money ever reached the little guys.
gao-gaoreports-gao-07-738t: No Child Left Behind's tutoring promise needed work in 2007 — GAO's briefing says better federal moves could lift the supplemental-services rollout. The testimony targets the implementation gaps. The findings ask whether the extra help reached the kids it was for.
gao-gaoreports-gao-07-778t: Forcing broke borrowers into credit counseling sounded good in 2007 — but GAO's briefing says nobody could prove the bankruptcy reform's classes helped. The testimony questions the mandate's payoff. The findings' verdict: a feel-good rule with no evidence it changed any debtor's fate.
gao-gaoreports-gao-07-798t: Loan guarantees for energy moonshots needed watching in 2007 — GAO's briefing eyes the new program backing innovative technology with taxpayer money. The testimony probes the rollout for weak spots. The findings ask whether the public's bet on breakthroughs was being managed with real care.
gao-gaoreports-gao-07-838t: The federal top ranks were still pale and male in 2007 — GAO's briefing examines diversity in the Senior Executive Service and the Postal Service's upper levels. The testimony puts numbers to the gap. The findings ask whether the government's leadership looked like the governed.
gao-gaoreports-gao-07-858t: The drug-discount sign-up was working, slowly, in 2007 — GAO's briefing says approvals for the low-income subsidy had improved, but finding the rest stayed hard. The testimony balances progress and gaps. The findings' plea: the poorest should not miss the help built for them.
gao-gaoreports-gao-07-898t: Kids were guinea pigs by default in 2007 — GAO's briefing examines the push to properly study and label drugs for children. The testimony tracks the pediatric research incentives. The findings argue that small patients deserve tested medicines, not hand-me-down doses.
gao-gaoreports-gao-07-948t: Homeland Security's buying machine was still being built in 2007 — GAO's briefing says standing up a real acquisition shop stayed hard. The testimony charts the growing pains in detail. The findings argue that a department is only as honest as its purchasing.
gao-gaoreports-gao-07-998t: Blue helmets versus Stars and Stripes in 2007 — GAO's briefing compares the costs, strengths, and limits of U.S. and UN peacekeeping side by side. The testimony lays the ledgers next to each other. The findings inform the eternal question: whose boots on the ground, and whose bill?
gao-gaoreports-gao-08-108t: GAO warned Congress in 2007 that germ labs were breeding faster than the rulebook. The high-security sites that handle the world's worst bugs were popping up with thin federal tracking, GAO found. The briefing raised the uneasy question of the decade: who watches the labs, when the labs hold the stuff of nightmares?
gao-gaoreports-gao-08-1148t: A GAO official laid out findings on secure Border Initiative: DHS Needs to Address Significant Risks in Delivering Key Technology Investment for Congress in 2008. Its findings feed into Congress's hearings and new laws. Its conclusions can shape how agencies run their programs.

gao-gaoreports-gao-08-118t: GAO briefed Congress in 2007 on the flood insurance plan's money woes: deep in the red after big storms, charging too little to cover its bets. Cut-rate premiums and repeat payouts to the same soggy homes kept the books bleeding. The briefing sketches a program drowning in the very risk it was built to tame.
gao-gaoreports-gao-08-138t: This 2007 Government Accountability Office testimony reviews U.S. programs to help other countries build capacity for tracking infectious diseases. American agencies were funding surveillance systems abroad so outbreaks could be spotted early — protecting both those nations and the United States. GAO assesses how the programs were working and where the global disease-detection network still had blind spots.
gao-gaoreports-gao-08-208t: GAO warned Congress in 2007 that Project Bioshield — the stockpile of drugs and shots against germ attacks — was flirting with old blunders. Rushed buys and loose handling had burned the program before. The briefing urges a steadier hand this time: learn the past lessons, or the nation's germ-attack cupboard will stay half-bare when it counts.
gao-gaoreports-gao-08-218t: This 2007 Government Accountability Office testimony provides updated information on freight railroad rates and industry trends. With railroads consolidating and shipping costs rising, GAO's data gave Congress a factual baseline for debates over rail regulation. The testimony covers how rates were moving and what the trends meant for farmers, manufacturers, and consumers who depend on rail freight.
gao-gaoreports-gao-08-228t: Looking past Iraq, GAO told Congress in 2007 that the next rebuild job needed a real playbook. Patching up broken nations had stretched every agency thin, yet no shared plan told them how to work as one. The briefing calls for a government-wide game plan — so the next mission starts with a map instead of making it up on the fly.
gao-gaoreports-gao-08-238t: A 2007 Government Accountability Office report commenting on proposed legislation to create a bipartisan task force on the nation's long-term fiscal challenge. With entitlement spending and debt on an unsustainable path, GAO weighed in on whether the task-force approach could force action. The report frames the fiscal cliff ahead and evaluates the bill's design as a way to break Washington's budget paralysis.
gao-gaoreports-gao-08-248t: Delivered as 2007 testimony, this Government Accountability Office report tackles the question of which public employees are covered by Social Security. Millions of state and local government workers sit outside the system under various exemptions, creating coverage gaps and fiscal questions. GAO outlines the issues for lawmakers weighing whether to expand coverage or leave the patchwork in place.
gao-gaoreports-gao-08-268t: This 2007 Government Accountability Office testimony explains the Congressional Review Act — the law that lets Congress overturn federal agency regulations within a window after they are issued. GAO, which reports to Congress on each major rule, describes how the review process works and how often lawmakers have actually used it. The testimony serves as a plain-language briefing on one of Congress's sharper oversight tools.
gao-gaoreports-gao-08-278t: GAO gave Congress an early read in 2007 on a team-up idea: pair the Small Business Administration's loan smarts with the farm agency's small-town reach. Merging SBA know-how with rural outposts could put more loan help in far-flung towns. The briefing weighs the prize — more rural firms funded — against the drag of meshing two unlike shops.
